unit.title: Electricity
unit.blurb: Circuits, conductors and insulators, safety, switches, and brighter or dimmer bulbs.

O1.t: Build a simple circuit, and sort materials into electrical conductors and insulators.

O2.t: Know that water can conduct electricity, and follow rules for using electricity safely.

O3.t: Explain why plugs, wires and tools use both conductors and insulators.

O4.t: Know that a switch opens and closes a gap in a circuit to turn it off and on.

O5.t: Predict how adding batteries or bulbs changes how bright bulbs are (or how loud a buzzer is).

captions: Hello, electric explorers!
Let's make a bulb light up!
This is lesson 6.1: which materials conduct electricity?
We need a battery, some wires and a bulb.
Join them in a loop, with no gaps.
The bulb lights up!
This loop is called a circuit. Electricity flows round it.
Pause and think.
What must a circuit be like for the bulb to light?
Let's put different things in a gap in the circuit.
A metal paper clip. The bulb lights!
A wooden stick. No light. A plastic ruler. No light.
A metal spoon. It lights again! Metals let electricity through.
Materials that let electricity flow are called conductors.
Metals are good conductors.
Materials that stop electricity are called insulators.
Plastic, wood and rubber are insulators.
Did you know?
A wire has metal inside, to carry electricity.
And it has plastic outside, to keep our hands safe.
Joke time!
Why was the electric eel so good at its job?

Your turn.
Which material is a conductor?

Put different things in the gap: a coin, a crayon, a key.
Does the bulb light? Then it is a conductor!
Let's remember.
A circuit is a complete loop, with no gaps.
Conductors let electricity flow.
Metals are good conductors.
Plastic, wood and rubber are insulators. Electric work!

captions: Hello, electric explorers!
How do we turn things on and off?
This is lesson 6.4: switches.
Press a light switch. Click! The light comes on.
Press it again. Click! The light goes off.
On, off, on, off!
How does a switch work?
A switch can close the circuit or open it.
When the switch is closed, there is no gap. Electricity flows, and the bulb is on.
When the switch is open, there is a gap. Electricity stops, and the bulb is off.
Pause and think.
When a switch is open, is the bulb on or off?
Switches are everywhere!
A TV remote has switches inside.
A torch has a switch. Your toys have on-off switches.
And a doorbell is a switch too. Ding dong!
Did you know?
Turning off lights when you leave a room saves energy.
Be an energy saver!
Riddle time!
I have a switch, and I light up your room. What am I?
A lamp!
Your turn.
What does a switch do when you turn the light off?
Let's make a switch, with an adult.
Push two drawing pins into a piece of card, and join them into a circuit.
Hook a paper clip on one pin.
Swing the clip to touch the other pin. On! Swing it away. Off!
Let's remember.
A switch turns a circuit on and off.
When a switch is closed, there is no gap, and the bulb is on.
When a switch is open, there is a gap, and the bulb is off.
And switches are everywhere! Switched-on work!

captions: Hello, electric explorers!
What happens if we add more parts to a circuit?
This is lesson 6.5: changing the number of components.
The parts of a circuit are called components.
A battery is a component. So is a bulb.
A buzzer is a component that makes a sound.
And a switch is a component too.
Pause and think.
What do we call the parts of a circuit?
Start with one battery and one bulb.
Now add another battery.
The bulb gets brighter!
More batteries give more push to the electricity. A buzzer gets louder too.
Now keep one battery, and add more bulbs.
With one bulb, it is bright.
With two bulbs, each one is dimmer.
The same battery has to share its energy.
Did you know?
If you add too many batteries, the bulb can get too hot and burn out. Pop!
Joke time!
Why did the battery go to the party?
To get charged up!
Your turn.
What happens to the bulb if you add another battery?
Let's test it, with an adult.
Make a circuit with one battery and one bulb.
Add another battery. Is the bulb brighter?
Now add another bulb. Are the bulbs dimmer?
Let's remember.
The parts of a circuit are called components.
More batteries make a bulb brighter.
More bulbs, with the same battery, make each bulb dimmer.
And a buzzer gets louder with more batteries. Electrifying work! You have finished the Stage 4 lessons!
